title: How Does a Convenience Store Arrange Its Shelves to Catch Your Eye, Your Heart and Your Money?
excerpt: Welcome. In here you'll find a city's consumer habits and its trends.
body:
Welcome. In here you'll find a city's consumer habits and its trends.

FamilyMart, 7-Eleven and Lawson are the three Japanese convenience store chains doing best in China, and the one most copied is 7-Eleven, with its "striped signboard."

The knockoffs give themselves away with their fake-looking storefronts and lighting that is never bright enough, but the off-key feeling peaks the moment you step inside. The shelves are either too empty or too messy. What you urgently need usually isn't there, and what is there you may never want to buy. By "you" we mainly mean young people.

With retail in a broad slump, how do convenience stores hold on to shoppers? We have already explained [how this model flourished in Japan](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/13453.html), and shared [19 secrets of convenience stores, from who likes to shop in them to how they choose their locations](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/19436.html). This time we want to show how each product in a convenience store finds its way in front of the shopper.

In the end, people go to convenience stores for one reason: the stores have what they want. To find out how, we spent time in several FamilyMart and 7-Eleven stores and talked with a few store managers and staff.

"Only the most popular, best-selling products make it into a convenience store," Wang Yiwen, spokesperson for FamilyMart China, told QDaily. Shelf space in a convenience store is "extremely, extremely sought after. If a product doesn't perform, it gets pulled."

Take FamilyMart. A store has roughly 2,000 to 3,000 products it can rotate in and out, and the weakest sellers are cut: a product that sells poorly lasts no more than three months on the shelf, and over a year more than half the range is replaced.

At the same time, how does a store of just over 100 square meters cover such a sprawling range of needs?

![Shelves inside a convenience store](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160726150742AwMsxnbTVD7pyKUY.jpg-w600)

A pair of stockings for an emergency, or medical iodine swabs; a small bottle of MOSCATO sparkling wine to take to a friend's place; a sudden whim for a salted soft-boiled egg... How do all these items, each in its own category, end up under one roof?

Have you noticed that convenience store shelves are always packed full, yet look orderly, so that whatever you want is easy to spot?

The craft behind this is our subject here: "the display logic of convenience stores." It takes cooperation among the merchandising, marketing and training departments, among others, and it is not something small, unbranded shops without scale can easily pick up.

We also found that convenience stores in different business districts and of different formats sell different things; that different refrigerated cases are set to different temperatures; and that convenience store snacks come in different packaging from hypermarket snacks, with small packs steadily catching on...

Convenience stores follow their customers' needs closely. They also set out, deliberately, to shape what customers buy and how.

## A Loop-Shaped Store Makes Sure You Pass Certain Shelves

A standard convenience store usually has about 100 to 120 square meters of usable floor space. Stores adjust their fittings to their size; 7-Eleven's very small stores, for instance, have special raised shelves.

Unlike a corner grocery, a convenience store rarely makes you double back. You go from the entrance past the cashier counter, all the way to the chilled daily-delivery goods at the back, and out the door again: one full loop. Unless they come in for something specific, most shoppers walk this route once around.

![Floor plan of a convenience store](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607261507435Q796XoDayqmrSY3.jpg-w600)

Floor plan based on the FamilyMart K11 store

Along this "main path" you pass the "promotional end-cap" the store pushes hardest, the shelf of own-brand products, and the fresh food section, which brings in 40% of a convenience store's revenue. Non-daily-delivery goods and sundries sit in the middle of the loop, and magazines go by the window.

The cashier counter is usually on one side of the door, and the door is rarely in the middle of the storefront, so customers can take the shortest path out after paying.

Counters for loose ready-to-eat items such as oden and steamed buns sit right next to the cashier counter, usually beside a backup cooler of drinks, nudging shoppers to buy a drink with their food.

Most daily-delivery goods (also called fresh food) must be sold chilled, and refrigerated shelving has to stand against a wall. So daily-delivery goods usually line one side of the store, while the opposite wall holds the cash register and counter.

## Light on Top, Heavy Below: Products People Come In For Go Down Low

One rule of stocking convenience store shelves is to go from small to large and light to heavy, top to bottom. Large jugs of Nongfu Spring water and big boxes of pull-out tissues, for example, mostly sit on the bottom shelf.

"Visually, if it's top-heavy, there really is a problem. And if it's a small item, putting it at the bottom makes it even harder to see," Wang Yiwen told QDaily.

Depending on how the goods are packaged, convenience store shelves carry hooks, and some even have a "shelf within a shelf."

![A shelf with hooks and a shelf within a shelf](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703121827zoUYOvCaNJ5VyBch.jpg-w600)

"Integrated shelving is where display is heading. It lets small items from different categories sit neatly together," Wang Yiwen said. The first rule of convenience store display is to let customers see as many products as possible.

There are exceptions. Light, small items such as lighters and stockings also go on inconspicuous bottom shelves. "Think about it: how desperate must someone be to buy stockings at a convenience store? They'll find them wherever you put them."

![Emergency items on the bottom shelf](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703121827z3Ov2phTLFBfRVuD.jpg-w600)

Emergency items such as Band-Aids, tissues and lighters are on the bottom shelf

The same logic applies to the drinks cooler. In winter, stores give the best shelf positions to fashionable "light-flavor waters" such as Qinning Water and Haijing Lemon, to steer what people buy. Strong brands such as cola go in slightly less noticeable spots, for the same reason: "Someone who wants a cola will find it wherever you put it."

"Demand for drinks falls, so we have to do more to guide shoppers with the display," Wang Yiwen explained. "Then in summer (when all drinks sell well), I just put the best-selling cola in the most visible spot with the most facings."

Drinks, sandwiches and rice balls in the refrigerated cases are also things people come in specifically to buy. Shoppers have made up their minds well before they arrive, so these products don't need prominent spots near the door to steer them.

## Every Convenience Store Has One Shelf That Changes More Than Any Other

Once you are inside, the first shelf facing the cashier counter is the store's "prime real estate." Every customer has to pass it, and they inevitably linger there while queuing to pay.

FamilyMart calls this shelf the "promotional end-cap," and 7-Eleven calls it the "special display shelf." Either way, it gets special attention.

Nothing on this shelf is there by chance. At FamilyMart, for example, the top tier currently holds a Spring Festival promotion and the second holds topical products, such as movie merchandise for *Star Wars* and *Kung Fu Panda*. Further down: "buy one, get one free," "20% off when you buy two"... every product has a promotional tag in front of it.

![The promotional end-cap in a FamilyMart store](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703121828sq1zoJ8rfhS5FXta.jpg-w600)

The "promotional end-cap" in a FamilyMart store

"We work with manufacturers when choosing promotional products, but we also make our own picks. With Spring Festival coming, for example, we're pushing more snacks such as jerky and roasted nuts," FamilyMart told QDaily.

"The special display shelf is the shelf 7-Eleven updates most often. On average its products change every two to three weeks," said Wu Meng, head of the administrative headquarters at 7-Eleven Beijing. Promotional products "are generally new products and the best products. Only if customers get to know these best products is there a chance of building a habit of buying them again and again."

## Did You Notice? The Bread Box Is Tilted to Match the Shelf

Convenience store products fall into three groups: daily-delivery goods (fresh food delivered every day, such as rice balls, sandwiches and boxed meals), non-daily-delivery goods (longer-lasting items such as instant noodles and potato chips), and non-food sundries.

Daily-delivery goods come from factories that supply only convenience stores, which means the recipes, and even the packaging, are carefully designed and owned exclusively by the chain.

FamilyMart delivers fresh food twice a day and everything else once a day. After the lunch rush, sandwiches, sushi and the store's own bread run short to varying degrees. On the bread shelf, staff pack the top two rows tightly, in order of priority from highest to lowest, to keep the shelf looking as full as possible.

![Boxed bread standing on the shelf](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160726150744ME0ag34cw2mFYpDr.jpg-w600)

Boxed bread that can "stand" on its own

In some rows only one loaf is left, yet it is still pushed to the very front, level with the other rows. Oddly, this lone loaf stands upright by itself, with nothing propping it up from behind.

Look closely at the shelf and you will see that the box inside the packaging is angled to match the slope of the shelf. With no outside help, the bread "stands" upright and shows customers the whole package.

Last October, FamilyMart launched its "Black Label series" of boxed meals. The biggest difference from conventionally packaged meals is that you can see the food inside at a glance.

Huge chicken drumsticks, carefully arranged plating... every Black Label meal comes in transparent packaging in place of the old printed pictures of the dish. FamilyMart plans to extend the Black Label series to more kinds of food, all in the same black packaging, to signal a different level of quality.

## Why Are the Refrigerated Cases Always Against the Wall?

The row of refrigerated cases along a convenience store wall has two kinds: open-front cases, called open-case, and glass-door cases, called walk-in. Both are set to 4 degrees Celsius, give or take 2 degrees.

The open cases hold drinks and food with short shelf lives, which the store must sell quickly. An open case is more inviting: easier to approach and to reach into.

![Open-front refrigerated cases](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031218286lg3vUBsaWYqN5Dz.jpg-w600)

What is harder to understand is that the other 4-degree case holds only shelf-stable drinks (drinks that need no refrigeration in transit). Why sell mineral water from a fridge even in winter?

"Ten years ago, when Shanghai first got convenience stores, lots of people would come and ask, 'Why are all your drinks in the fridge? Get me one at room temperature.' Now very few ask."

According to Wang Yiwen, the practice came from Japan: "In developed countries and regions people drink more cold drinks, especially carbonated drinks like cola, which taste better cold."

People are getting more used to cold drinks, especially the young shoppers convenience stores care most about.

"But go inland and lots of people come and ask again, just like ten years ago. That's interesting."

Another benefit of putting the cases against the wall is that the storeroom is right behind them. Look closely and you will see that the walk-in connects to the storeroom, where backup drinks sit on shelves behind the case, already chilling and ready to restock at any time.

So even in summer, when people drink vast amounts of cold drinks, a shopper who opens the fridge at any hour can get a thoroughly chilled drink.

![Drinks in a walk-in refrigerated case](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031218295BnsgUrPzSf3Jv0T.jpg-w600)

## Why Does the Winter Hot-Drink Case Hold Only Small Bottles?

Have you noticed that hot drinks all come in small bottles?

Besides the milk tea, coffee and soy milk made fresh in-store, convenience stores bring out a small hot-drink case in winter, usually from November to the following March.

![A hot-drink case](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703121829U1buBVIZOXQAskLh.jpg-w600)

The canned hot drinks at the upper left come with cardboard sleeves

"In winter people want fewer drinks and less water, and drinking 500 milliliters at once is a bit much, so the sizes (of hot drinks) are set smaller," a FamilyMart employee told our reporter.

"Set," not "picked": hot-drink bottles have to be specially developed to meet safety requirements such as heat resistance. The hot-drink case runs at about 55 degrees, so to keep the cans from burning people's hands, canned drinks get a cardboard sleeve.

When each bottle goes into the hot-drink case, it gets a label on its base marking the date by which it is safe to drink.

Temperature has a big effect on the quality of food and drinks. A room-temperature drink might normally keep for nine months, but in the hot-drink case it lasts only about 14 days. Shelf lives vary by product; the shortest is just seven days.

![Labels on the bases of hot-drink bottles](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703121830EBjmYOGUonyA18Kg.jpg-w600)

## Why Are Convenience Stores Full of Poor-Value Small Packs?

Bigger packs of food are usually better value. In hypermarkets we often see promotional packs such as "family value sharing pack" and "buy three, get two free": the more they sell, the better, and every purchase feels like a bargain. In convenience stores you rarely see them.

The trend in convenience stores is small packs. Miaofu cakes, sold one at a time. 3+2 sandwich crackers, sold two at a time.

![Small packs of cakes and biscuits](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160726150745nsHJPhUmvDyxN0lp.jpg-w600)Small packs of cakes and biscuits

![Small packs of own-brand products](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703121830HpT89FIvoQdq4LKZ.jpg-w600)

Small packs of own-brand products

![Small packs of candy](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160726150746XFYWj2ArDK3BJRHo.jpg-w600)

Small packs of candy

One reason is limited display space: for a convenience store, shelf space is a luxury.

Another is that convenience store shoppers are not price-sensitive and don't mind a difference of a few yuan or a few jiao. For them, getting through a whole roll of Oreos is the more daunting prospect.

Take the FamilyMart K11 store, next to an office building: white-collar workers and other business people are its main customers. Two biscuits and a cup of coffee make just the right afternoon tea.

To suit shoppers who prefer "small, frequent meals," FamilyMart began selling sushi by the piece last autumn and winter. Shoppers pick pieces one by one, mixing flavors as they like, and once they have four they get a box to take them away in.

![Sushi sold by the piece](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031218300yHF8OXbzmLh31iS.jpg-w600)

## Different Locations, Different Things on the Shelves

Even stores of the same brand sell somewhat different things depending on location and format. FamilyMart stores near hospitals, for example, stock more congee, while the K11 store next to an office building mainly pushes the premium "Black Label series" boxed meals.

![Refrigerated cases at the FamilyMart K11 store](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703121831vN58gpztCGmOK17d.jpg-w600)Taken at the FamilyMart K11 store

The refrigerated cases at K11 look striking, with a whole row of Bernachon coffee in every color. At an ordinary neighborhood store, Bernachon gets only three facings.

"I haven't seen that many facings of Perrier and pure fruit juice at any other store. At a location like this, they won't put mineral water in the refrigerated case," said Wang Yiwen, for whom visiting convenience stores is part of the daily job.

![Refrigerated cases at the FamilyMart South Shaanxi Road Station store](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031218316webc5qI9SRrKLdM.jpg-w600)Taken at the FamilyMart South Shaanxi Road Station store

FamilyMart sets up every type of shelf in a showroom. "Everyone has to go and see it once, and we explain to store managers why we are pushing these products this season." Since most of its stores are franchises, this is how FamilyMart puts its display philosophy into practice.

Product display is part of the training for new store staff. Full-time employees get six days of training; part-timers get two.

Store managers can adjust which categories they order and how much, but what really decides it is the tastes and spending power of the customers they are targeting.

FamilyMart's store design in China is now in its third generation, with warmer natural wood replacing the original white shelves and floors. Alongside the traditional full row of refrigerated cases, third-generation stores add island cases, giving customers more case space to choose fresh food such as sushi, sandwiches and boxed meals.

Apart from subway and airport stores, most third-generation FamilyMart stores over 100 square meters have a seating area with 10 to 20 seats. "The longer people sit, the more they (may) spend." Even after mealtime, customers who had bought fresh-brewed coffee or oden were still sitting in the FamilyMart K11 store, and even in the dead of winter people were buying from the Fami soft-serve ice cream machine.

![An advertisement for China Guangfa Bank inside the store](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703121832UnJdCaLWeN9pfz7E.jpg-w600)

An advertisement for China Guangfa Bank in the store

Over two hours, the FamilyMart store played more than 20 popular songs without a single repeat, with a weather forecast broadcast in between. The screen in front of the cashier counter cycled nonstop between FamilyMart's promotional film and video ads from partner brands.

"Convenience stores in Taiwan go even further: the cashier counter is covered in brands' ads," she said. Convenience stores have become one of the offline channels where brands launch new products, and Wang Yiwen, who is from Taiwan, knows better than most how much the convenience store platform matters to them.

(Graphics: Lin Yuyao. Reporter Fei Liting also contributed to this article.)
